body_markdown:
What you see here is called a roadster, even if it looks nothing like one. A roadster is defined as a two-seat vehicle without a roof, as stated in our[Car Design Glossary](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=Roadster%3A%20A%20roofless%2C%20two%20seat%20vehicle%20focusing%20on%20dynamic%20performance%20through%20a%20small%20footprint%2C%20often%20with%20an%20aggressively%20cab%20backward%20design.) . The original, Lotus Elise–derived Tesla Roadster (2008–12) embraced the definition, but Tesla is far from an ordinary company. These folks can make mistakes that would create class-action lawsuits for the likes of General Motors, and yet company stock price still appreciates. Perhaps Elon Musk was right when he said, “If you value Tesla as just an auto company, it’s just the wrong framework: If you ask the wrong question, then the right answer is impossible.”


Tesla is a tech company, with values akin to the social media juggernaut that[famously](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_Platforms#History:~:text=On%20May%202,%5B39%5D) *moved fast and broke things* . To my personal amazement over the last 16-or-so years, the business model actually works and its design team reaped the benefits. For starters, Tesla democratized the electric vehicle architecture and made it OK to slap huge touchscreens on dashboards. The style present in its vehicles was subtle at best, boring at worst, but the[Cybertruck changed all that](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-2024-tesla-cybertruck/) .


Shockingly, the Cybertruck became a bit of a halo vehicle for the brand. And that’s one of the four points I would like to inject into the conversation about Tesla’s latest concept, because I reckon you haven’t considered them.


## More Lambo than a Lamborghini


Tesla


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


*That windshield! Oh my goodness, look at that windshield!*


We know the Roadster is heavily influenced by 50-year-old Lamborghinis, but I’d wager Tesla is doing the deed better than modern Lamborghinis are. My Vellum Venom rants on the[2022 Countach](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-2022-lamborghini-countach-lpi-800-4/#:~:text=Look%20up%20a,adjacent%20to%20it.) and the[Huracán Sterrato](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-2024-lamborghini-huracan-sterrato/#:~:text=The%20cowl%20is,painted%20body%20panels.) include Lambo’s inauthentic DNA application around the[cowl](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=Cowl%3A%20The%20base%20of%20the%20windshield%2C%20and%20a%20flashpoint%20of%20significant%20cost%20and%20functionality%20for%20modern%20car%20design.) . Do the cowl wrong and the whole car struggles to keep its head above water (so to speak). In the case of the 2022 Countach, Lamborghini added dark elements to the back of the hood to mimic the shape of the original Countach windshield.


That certainly checks off a box in one’s DNA assessment, but Tesla dug deeper and did it better. The Roadster’s aggressively tapered fenders give the body the equivalent of “pursed lips” on a human, but it flows better when an aggressive sheet of glass is the starting point of your tapering. It’s cleaner, easier to process, and simply beautiful to admire.


Tesla


Tesla


Tesla


There’s an argument that the Roadster isn’t a production vehicle, especially as it’s been vaporware since 2017. A fair point, but the hype around this one is hard to ignore.


What we see in the pictures above proves that a properly shaped hunk of glass evokes imagery far easier than over-styled body panels and an overdose of tacked-on hexagonal elements (like taillights in the newest Lamborghinis). Adding “Lambo” doors also helped, but cars have a core, just like the human body. That core is the cowl. If you do it right, you can make anything look sleek and sporty. *Especially from the front.*


## The Real Reason It Isn’t a Roadster?


Tesla


Tesla


I’d prefer Tesla called this a coupe, but that’s just a purist being picky in a world of tech disruptors who couldn’t care less about tradition. Tesla gave the original 2017 concept a removable targa panel. The full-on rejection of roadster DNA in 2026 suggests something else is going on behind the scenes.


I reckon this involves platform sharing. Any automaker who builds at scale must embrace the practice, and the highly successful Model Y crossover proves Tesla already knows the drill.


Mecum


Pontiac


Tesla


Tesla


This has probably boosted profit and prestige since the horse-drawn carriage era, but we should thank General Motors for the modern application of platform sharing. It turned a respectable A-body Pontiac LeMans/GTO into an aesthetically assertive G-body Grand Prix personal luxury coupe, with just a few tweaks to the platform.


With the G-body in mind, take a critical look at the[volumes](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=Volumes%3A%20The%20basic%20shape%20of%20a%20vehicle%2C%20the%C2%A0outline%20of%20the%20body%20work%20when%20seen%20from%20the%20side.%20More%20info%20here.) of both the Cybercab and the Roadster. Focus on the scissor doors (which likely require reinforcement in the same place), and the length between the rear wheels and the doors. This suggests similarities in the chassis, which is logical considering both are smaller vehicles that still need to hold a requisite amount of electrons to do their jobs.


Even the painted surfaces around the quarter windows are similar. It’s almost as if Tesla delayed the Roadster’s introduction to ensure it shared mass-production DNA with the Cybercab.


Tesla


Tesla


As GM did with the G-body, Tesla extended the space[between the front door and the front wheel](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=Dash%2Dto%2Daxle%20%5Bratio%5D%3A%20The%20distance%20between%20the%20centerline%20of%20the%20front%20wheel%20and%20the%20bottom%20of%20the%20windshield.%20More%20info%20here.) . This likely provided more functional space for high-performance engineering, ensured a sleeker roofline, and gave “permission” to lengthen every line radiating outward from the cowl to allow for that prestigious Gandini-Lamborghini flavor we’ve loved since the 1970s.


I’ve had the pleasure to see Cybercabs in traffic. Societal implications of their existence aside, they are slick machines thanks to their low slung demeanor. It works, but the Cybercab is worthy of further elongation into a flagship vehicle. Even if the Roadster doesn’t make production, it pays homage to the tricks Harley Earl did in his career at General Motors. Like the Buick Y-job before it, Tesla’s use of “longer, lower, and wider” proves the notion still has a place in our SUV-heavy society.


## Brand DNA


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Tesla


Tesla


I will keep this one short, as the Cybertruck’s aggressively angular design was hot enough to generate around 2 million pre-orders. Tesla had a great kernel, but it only germinated in new products.


The Cybertruck’s now-iconic fascias are plastered on everything from the high-volume Model Y Juniper to the high-technology Cybercab and Roadster. I can’t help but feel like this controversial truck is getting the last laugh on all its haters.


## An Attention to Detail


Google


Anadolu via Getty Images


Tesla


Cybertruck aside, companies in the tech space that dabble (as it were) in automobiles have a habit of making utterly creative machines. My favorite was the Koala/Firefly autonomous vehicle from Google, as it gave a VW “people’s car” vibe without actually being influenced by said insect.


The Zoox Robotaxi looks like a single pod from a[Disney People Mover](https://www.fly2houston.com/airport-business/newsroom/articles/item/the-disney-built-subway-beneath-bush-airport-turns-45/) , prioritizing function over form. I worry about those corner-mounted wheels in densely populated areas, but the design clearly puts cabin space as a top concern.


Tesla’s 2026 Roadster brings a wow factor akin to that of the Countach back in the 1970s, but it’s very heavy handed in its retro inspirations. The 2013 Model S was a completely different animal, as very little besides its silhouette was influenced by Mercedes’ CLS coupe. Its EV architecture made hatchbacks cool again, and the proportioning was spot-on for a luxury car.


Lamborghini


Tesla


Part of the problem comes from something our own[Matteo Licata](https://www.hagerty.com/media/design/design-professor-teslas-futuristic-roadster-is-also-a-throwback/) noted, as the “Roadster’s surfacing makes the whole design feel a tad underbaked.” Licata also popped in a photo of the original Countach in his story, just so you can see how much time was spent surfacing the original.


So I added the same picture, and it’s clear which car looks like it spent months in a clay-modeling studio, and which car looks like it was designed with software assistance and aggressive shadowing as inspiration. The problem with the Tesla Roadster is also that of its Cybertruck stablemate: It needs more time for designers to obsess over its surfaces.


My goal here was to present four points pertaining to the Tesla Roadster’s design, which excels in some aspects and feels undercooked in others. Bonus if I’ve inspired you to think more critically about car design in general. That is always the aim. As always, thanks for reading.
